drainage.local_h: Water on flat ground, sand on top and clay below
local: Kilgore's sandy topsoil can fool you. Water soaks in fast, so the yard looks fine in a light rain. Then it hits clay or a hardpan layer underneath and has nowhere to go. On a flat lot it spreads sideways, ponds in the low corner or pools against the slab. The worst spots are usually where a downspout empties. Heavy storms are when the problem shows, which is why we like to walk the property during or right after a rain.

We trace the water first. Where does it come from, where does it sit and where could it leave? Then you get a written estimate that says what we are installing and why. A downspout extension or solid-pipe reroute handles many yards. A regrade of one low spot or a swale handles others. Catch basins, channel drains and pop-up emitters cover the middle ground. A French drain with sock-wrapped pipe and #57 stone is the answer when water must be collected underground.

The hard part on a flat Kilgore lot is the outlet. A drain needs a steady fall toward somewhere the water can actually leave: daylight, a curb, a lower part of the lot or a pop-up emitter. Corrugated pipe in a rock bag, laid shallow with no outlet, silts up in a season or two. So we dig with a real fall, backfill with stone so clay fines cannot clog it, and cap the trench with soil and sod or river rock.

Most Kilgore fixes can be done without tearing up the yard. Pricing follows linear feet of pipe, dig depth and access, outlet, catch basins and the finish on top. Small fixes run $450 to $1,000, a standard single run $1,900 to $3,000, full systems $3,000 to $4,500 and large combined projects $4,500 and up. Digging goes faster in a dry stretch. Doing it before the spring rains means one less season with a pond in the back corner.

faq.q: Why does my Kilgore yard flood when the soil is sandy?
faq.a: Sand soaks water in quickly, but clay or hardpan underneath stops it. On a flat lot, the water then spreads sideways and ponds. Downspouts that empty onto the surface make it worse. The fix is to give the water a path to somewhere it can leave.

faq.q: Can you fix drainage without tearing up my yard?

faq.q: Where does the water go once it is collected?

fertilization.local_h: Why Kilgore soil needs a test before a bag
local: Decades of fallen pine needles have pushed a lot of Kilgore soil acidic, and the sand underneath lets water and fertilizer wash straight through. Together those two facts explain why a lawn can get fed every spring and still look hungry. Low pH keeps grass from using what you put down, and the sand carries the rest below the roots. So we pull a soil sample first and build the plan from the numbers, adding lime only where the test calls for it.

Slow-release nitrogen matters more on sand than on almost any other soil in our area. A quick-release shot gets rinsed past the roots by the next heavy rain, so we use slower-release products and time them to soil temperature. The first feeding goes down around April 25, once overnight lows hold above 60 and the grass is fully awake. Feed in March and most of it washes out, because bermuda and St. Augustine are still half-dormant and cannot pull it in.

Shade changes the plan on a Kilgore lawn. St. Augustine under pecans and pines grows slower and uses less than a full-sun bermuda yard, so pushing it hard only feeds weak growth. We set the program around the grass type and how much canopy sits over it. A summer-safe feeding goes down in early July, and the last nitrogen goes down in the first two weeks of September, before the grass heads toward dormancy. Late nitrogen on St. Augustine fuels large patch in October.

The last two pieces are aeration and the fall feeding. Lawns packed down by years of traffic get core aeration between late August and mid-September, with the feeding right behind it. In October a potassium-heavy winterizer goes down for cold hardiness, and next year's plan adjusts to what the soil test and the lawn showed. Beds in Kilgore benefit from the same thinking, since compost in the beds holds moisture that the sand would otherwise let go.

faq.q: How much does fertilizing a Kilgore lawn cost?
faq.a: Visits start from about $190. Multi-visit seasonal programs are priced on your lawn size and how many rounds it needs. Lawn size, grass type, lime after a soil test and adding core aeration all move the number. You get the plan and the price in writing before the first application goes down.

faq.q: How do I know if my Kilgore soil needs lime?
faq.a: You test it. Pine needles and sandy ground push many Kilgore yards acidic, but not every one, and lime only helps when the pH is actually low. We pull a sample, read the result and put lime in the plan only if the numbers call for it, so you do not pay for something the lawn does not need.

faq.q: Why not fertilize in March when the stores stack it up front?
faq.a: Those schedules were written for cool-season lawns up north. Bermuda and St. Augustine are still half-dormant in March and cannot use the nitrogen, so on Kilgore's sandy soil most of it washes out with the next rain. We wait until the grass is awake, around the end of April.

faq.q: Does a shaded St. Augustine lawn under pecans need the full program?
faq.a: Usually less. A shaded lawn grows slower and uses less nitrogen, so we tune the visits to the canopy and the soil test instead of running every round. The plan is written out before we start, so you see what goes down, when, and why.

faq.q: Do you aerate lawns in Kilgore?

hedge-trimming.local_h: Keeping Kilgore hedges tight without cutting bare wood
local: Kilgore's long, humid growing season keeps boxwoods, hollies and ligustrums pushing new growth from spring clear into fall. A foundation hedge trimmed once in the spring is shaggy by August and growing into window screens and across the walk. Most hedges here want two to three trims between spring and fall. June is the clean window for hollies and boxwoods, and we shape them often enough to stay tight without cutting back into bare wood that will not regrow.

Kilgore's acidic ground suits azaleas, and many East Texas yards have them. They are the shrub that punishes bad timing. Azaleas and mophead hydrangeas set next year's buds on this year's stems within weeks of finishing their show, so a trim in July or later gives you a green bush with no color. Early to mid June is the last clean shot, and right after bloom is the only safe time. We check what each shrub is before a blade touches it.

Shrubs under the big trees grow lopsided, because they lean toward whatever light gets through. On a lot with pecans and pines overhead, we shape each hedge a little wider at the base so the lower branches keep their leaves, and we do not shear it into a flat box. Tarps go down first, since pine needles and pecan leaves tend to collect in the beds around the foundation. Every clipping is raked, blown out of the beds and hauled off.

At the walkthrough we count the shrubs, check how overgrown they are and note which ones flower on old wood. Ligustrum and other hedges that got away from a past owner can take a hard rejuvenation cut, and we tell you honestly which ones will come back. Skip heavy shearing in late fall, because the tender regrowth burns brown in the first cold snap. We can put you on a recurring trim schedule or come back when you call.

irrigation.local_h: Watering sand over clay without flooding one corner

lawn-maintenance.local_h: Mowing around Kilgore's pecans, post oaks and pines
local: The first thing we check on a Kilgore lawn is what hangs over it. The older streets around downtown and Kilgore College carry big pecans, post oaks and loblolly pines, and the shade they throw decides the grass. Most of those yards are St. Augustine, which we hold at three and a half to four inches through summer and never cut below three. Full-sun bermuda yards run about one to one and a half inches in spring and two to two and a half in summer. Tell us which you have and we set the deck to match.

Trees change the work as much as the grass does. Surface roots from pecans and oaks make a mower deck bounce, so we ride over them at the right height instead of scalping the ridge. Low limbs mean ducking and trimming by hand, and we string-trim around every trunk without nicking the bark. One corner of the lawn often grows slower than the rest because it sits in deeper shade. We do not cut that corner shorter to catch it up, because short grass in the shade just thins out.

Sandy soil is the other Kilgore factor. It drains fast, so a lawn scalped in July dries out quickly and the roots pull back to match the blade. Keeping the grass tall shades that sand and holds moisture longer. If a patch keeps browning or a low spot stays soft for days, we point it out on the visit while it is still small and cheap to fix, and we tell you plainly when the real problem is water and not mowing.

Mowing season runs from late March through October, with a cut every five to seven days in peak growth and every other week as it slows. Kilgore is close enough to Longview that weekly or bi-weekly visits are practical. Clippings go back into the turf, walks and drives get blown clean, and early fall leaves are mulched back into the lawn. Once the pecans start dropping heavy in November, that becomes a separate leaf cleanup that we quote on its own.

faq.q: Why does the grass under my pecan keep thinning even though it gets mowed?
faq.a: Usually shade and roots, not the mower. Bermuda needs full sun and fades under a canopy, while St. Augustine tolerates partial shade if it stays tall. Where the canopy is too dense for any grass, a mulched bed with shade plants works better. We keep the deck high and tell you when mowing cannot fix it.

faq.q: Do you mow on the Rusk County side of Kilgore too?

faq.q: My yard is half sun and half shade. How do you mow it?

leaf-removal.local_h: A pecan, post oak and pine drop, pass by pass
local: Kilgore carries a heavy leaf load, because so many older lots sit under pecans, post oaks and loblolly pines. Removal starts in the first half of November, when the volume roughly triples in a few days. Pine needles land on top of the oak and pecan leaves, and pecans add husks and small twigs to the mix. A mower bag cannot keep up with that, and a leaf blower alone just moves it to the neighbor's side of the fence.

On a wooded Kilgore lot with St. Augustine underneath, timing matters more than looks. St. Augustine grows from surface runners and stays partly green into the cold months, so a wet leaf mat smothers the very part of the plant that has to survive winter. That mat also sets up large patch, which shows up as dead circles in March that people blame on the cold. Heavy canopy over St. Augustine can need weekly clearing for three or four weeks.

Here is how a pass works. The crew blows leaves out of the lawn, the shrub beds and the rock beds onto the street or another paved surface the trailer can reach. We pull the leaf vacuum trailer up, vacuum it all, shred it about 10 to 1 and haul it away. No bags sit at the curb and nothing gets mulched in. Then we re-edge bed lines the leaves buried and clear the drive, walks and patio, and we can clear exterior gutters on the same visit.

Most Kilgore lots need a pass in mid-November, another in mid-December and a last one before spring green-up, since post oaks hold leaves and drop them into February. Before November the light drop is better mulched into the lawn with the mower. The flat price follows lot size, number of trees, how deep the leaves are, how many beds need clearing and how many passes we plan. After a storm, we do post-storm cleanups too.

faq.q: How much does leaf removal cost in Kilgore?
faq.a: It is one flat price for the job, quoted in writing after a free walkthrough and before we start. There are no bag fees and no hourly meter. The number follows lot size, how many trees you have, how deep the leaves are, how many beds need clearing and how many passes the lot will need through the season.

faq.q: Can I mulch the pecan and oak leaves into my lawn myself?
faq.a: A light first drop, yes, with two passes of a mower while the leaves are dry. If you can still see green grass when you finish, you did it right. A heavy pecan or oak drop is too much to mulch in place and mats down over the grass, so on those lots we collect it and haul it off.

faq.q: Do you leave the leaves in bags at the curb?
faq.a: No bags at all. We blow everything onto a paved surface the trailer can reach, vacuum it up, shred it about 10 to 1 and haul it away. The only thing left is a clean lawn, clear beds and swept walks and drives, with the bed lines re-edged where leaves had buried them.

faq.q: Do you clear the shrub beds and rock beds too?

mulch-installation.local_h: Mulching beds that catch needles all year
local: With heavy pine and oak cover over so much of Kilgore, beds catch leaves and needles all year, and that debris sits on top of the old mulch. So we start by clearing it, re-cutting the edges clean and pulling weeds by the root. Then we loosen the top inch of soil that has crusted over, so rain gets down to the roots instead of running off. A mulch layer laid on top of a debris mat just holds more water against the foundation.

Depth matters more than people expect. Every online calculator says three inches, a number written for snow country. In East Texas that much sheds light rain like a tarp, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover to eat roots. We lay 1 to 1.5 inches, raked even and tapered off at stems and trunks. Around a mature pecan or pine, mulch kept off the trunk matters most, and we never put fabric under it.

Kilgore's sand drains fast, so a fresh layer of mulch does real work. It slows evaporation and keeps the soil beneath it cooler through July, and as it breaks down it turns into organic matter that sandy soil sorely needs. Hardwood, cypress, cedar, and dyed black or brown are all options. Pine straw is available on request, and in a Kilgore yard with pines overhead it is a natural match for the trees already dropping it.

The best window is late April through mid-May, right after the spring growth flush and before the heat arrives. The second is late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down before the leaves drop. Under heavy pine cover the old layer disappears faster, so some Kilgore beds want it twice. You pay for what the beds need, because we measure the beds and check how much of the old layer is left.

faq.q: How much does mulch installation cost in Kilgore?
faq.a: Most bed refreshes run $600 to $2,400. The price follows square footage, number of beds, mulch type, how much edging and weed pulling the beds need and whether it is a full install or a thin top-dress. A fall top-dress over a layer that is still there usually costs a fraction of a full install.

faq.q: How often should Kilgore beds get new mulch?
faq.a: Once a year in spring for most beds, with a light fall top-off if leaves and needles have broken the old layer down. Under heavy pine cover the old mulch disappears faster, so some beds need it twice. We check what is left before quoting.

faq.q: Can I get pine straw instead of mulch?
faq.a: Yes. Pine straw is available on request, along with hardwood, cypress, cedar, and dyed black or brown mulch. In a yard with loblolly pines overhead, straw matches the trees already dropping needles into the beds. We lay it at an even depth and keep it off stems and trunks.

faq.q: Why do you lay 1 to 1.5 inches and not 3?
faq.a: East Texas does not get snow loads that pack mulch down. Three inches sheds light rain, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover. A properly prepped bed with 1 to 1.5 inches does the job, takes less material and costs less.

faq.q: Do you put fabric down before the mulch?
faq.a: No. Mulch is supposed to break down into soil, and fabric blocks that. Instead we pull weeds by the root, re-cut the edges, loosen the top inch of soil and lay mulch evenly. Kilgore's sandy beds especially need the organic matter that real mulch adds over time.

retaining-walls.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes, a family-owned and fully insured company based in Longview, builds retaining walls in Kilgore. local: Sand behaves differently from clay when you cut into a slope. Kilgore's sandy soil erodes and slumps once it is cut, and it keeps sliding until something holds it. A wall here has to do more than stack blocks. It needs a compacted base set below grade, gravel backfill and weep outlets that let water out before it undercuts the footing. Skip any of those and the first hard rain finds the weak spot.

Water is what moves walls, even in sandy ground. Kilgore's topsoil drains fast, but it often sits on clay or a hardpan layer, so water reaches that layer and runs sideways behind the wall. We put a gravel chimney and a perforated drain pipe at the bottom of every wall, with an outlet that actually leads somewhere. On taller walls we add geogrid reinforcement. If a wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough.

Not every slope needs a wall. If the grade is gentle, a regrade with plants or sod to hold the soil may be enough. Once the ground drops more than you can mow, or soil keeps washing onto a walk or drive, a wall is usually the fix. We measure the grade change and give you both options when both make sense. Short seating walls and terraced steps are another way to use a drop in a Kilgore yard.

We build segmental block, natural stone, boulder and timber walls, and we rebuild ones that are leaning or failing. Height, linear footage, material, excavation, drainage and geogrid drive the written estimate. A dry stretch is the best time to dig and compact. If a bank near your drive is already washing out, do not wait for the next stretch of spring rain. A wall that goes in with a patio or beds can be part of the same plan.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost in Kilgore?
faq.a: Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000. Height and length move the number most. A short garden wall starts at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. Material, excavation, drainage and geogrid on taller walls matter too. You get a written, itemized estimate after the walkthrough.

faq.q: Do I need a retaining wall or just a regrade?
faq.a: If the slope is gentle, a regrade with plants or sod may hold the soil. Once the ground drops more than you can mow, or soil keeps washing onto a walk or drive, a wall is usually the fix. We measure the grade and give you both options when both make sense.

faq.q: Why does sandy soil make walls harder?
faq.a: Sand slumps and erodes when it is cut, and it does not stay put under the weight of block on an undisturbed base. We dig below grade, compact a crushed stone base and backfill with gravel so the wall sits on firm ground, not loose sand.

faq.q: What happens behind the wall?
faq.a: Gravel backfill, a perforated drain pipe at the bottom and an outlet that leads water somewhere. Every wall gets this. On taller walls we add geogrid reinforcement. Water pressure is what makes walls lean, so drainage is not an extra.

faq.q: Can you rebuild a leaning wall?
faq.a: Yes. Rebuilds of leaning or failed walls are part of the service. We take the wall apart, fix the base and the drainage, and rebuild it course by course. A wall that has started to lean usually has a water problem behind it, so we look at that first.

sod-installation.local_h: Picking the right grass under Kilgore's trees
local: In Kilgore the sod question is rarely about the sod. It is about how much light actually reaches the ground. We walk the yard and note where the summer sun falls, not where it falls in January, when the pecans and post oaks are bare and every lot looks sunnier than it is. Then we recommend a grass, or a split, for each area. St. Augustine goes where the canopy covers the yard, and bermuda goes only where it gets full sun.

Some spots are not sod spots at all. St. Augustine needs roughly four hours of direct sun to hold up, and under a dense stand of pines or pecans no turf does well for long. We tell you that before you pay for sod. Those corners usually do better as a mulched bed with shade plants, which also costs less to maintain than turf that fades by August. A split of sod and beds often makes the whole yard look more finished.

Preparation is where Kilgore's soil shows up. We strip the old turf and weeds to bare soil, regrade and level, and till in two to three inches of compost or topsoil. On fast-draining sand that compost is what lets the new roots find moisture. Starter fertilizer goes down under the sod, seams are staggered and tight, and access for the pallets is part of the price. Small patch repairs and plug work cost less than a full-yard install.

Timing follows the grass. Bermuda goes down best from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September, when the ground is warm. St. Augustine needs four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy, so get it in by the end of September, because sod laid in November sits on the ground like a rug. Sand dries fast, so the watering schedule is half the job. You get a daily morning plan for two weeks, then a taper to deep, less frequent soaks.

faq.q: How much does sod cost in Kilgore?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet based on the square footage. Grass type, removal of old turf, grading and soil amendment, how the site drains and access for pallets all move the number. Small patch repairs cost less, and a full yard with heavy prep costs more.

faq.q: Will new sod grow under the trees in my Kilgore yard?
faq.a: It depends on the light. St. Augustine needs roughly four hours of direct sun and tolerates partial shade. Under a dense canopy no sod survives, and we will say so before you pay for it. Those spots do better as mulched beds, and a mix of sod in the lighter areas works well.

faq.q: Should I use bermuda or St. Augustine in Kilgore?
faq.a: Whichever matches your sun. Bermuda wants full sun and thins to dirt in shade. St. Augustine handles partial shade and is the usual pick under Kilgore's older trees. Many yards need both, so we recommend a split by area after watching where the sun actually falls in summer.

faq.q: When should I lay sod in Kilgore?
faq.a: Bermuda goes down from late April through August. St. Augustine goes down from May through September and needs four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy, so aim for the end of September. Laid in November, it sits on top of the ground and does not root.

faq.q: How do I water new sod in sandy soil?
faq.a: Water every morning for the first two weeks, then taper to deep, less frequent soaks once the roots take hold. Sand dries out fast, so skipping days in the first weeks is how new sod fails. We leave a written schedule with the install so you know the plan from day one.

tree-planting.local_h: Digging in sand, watering through the first summers
local: Digging is the easy part in Kilgore. The sandy topsoil opens up fast and drains freely, so we hand-dig wide, shallow holes, cut any circling roots and put the native soil back in. No bag of garden soil goes in the middle, since a pocket of different soil keeps roots circling inside it instead of reaching out. The root flare stays at grade or a touch high, and we finish with a watering basin and a mulch ring pulled back off the trunk.

Water is what decides whether a new Kilgore tree lives. Sand drains so freely that water runs past a young root ball quickly, and the ball itself dries out in a day or two of July heat. For the first couple of summers a new tree needs steady, deliberate watering at the ball. We hand you a written watering schedule, and on bigger installs we come back around the 30-day mark to check how it is establishing.

We plant in fall when we can, from September until around Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm for weeks after the air cools, so an October tree gets close to six months of root growth before summer, where an April tree gets about eight weeks. We plant year-round, but a spring tree asks more of you through its first summer. On open lots with no neighbors' trees to break the wind, we stake the tree. Elsewhere we usually do not.

The hardest question on an older Kilgore street is where. A new tree dug in tight under a mature pecan or post oak fights its roots for water and light, and the digging can hurt those roots. Small understory trees like redbud or dogwood can work at the edge of a canopy. For open ground we will talk through live oak, Shumard oak, magnolia, river birch and crepe myrtles, and we weigh mature size as heavily as species.

faq.q: How much does it cost to plant a tree in Kilgore?
faq.a: We quote after a walkthrough because the species and size of the tree drive most of the cost, along with how many trees you want and how easy the spot is to reach. The written quote spells out the tree, the planting and the aftercare plan, so you know what you are paying for before we start.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant a tree in Kilgore?
faq.a: Fall, from September until around Thanksgiving. Roots keep growing in warm soil after the air cools, so the tree has months of root under it before the first 100-degree day. We plant year-round, but a tree planted in April needs more watering and more attention through its first summer.

faq.q: Can I plant a tree right under my big pecan?
faq.a: Usually not. Digging under a mature pecan or oak damages its roots, and the new tree would be competing with them for water. We look for a spot at the edge of the canopy or in open ground where the new tree can grow without hurting the old one.

faq.q: Should I mix garden soil into the hole when planting?
faq.a: No. Native soil goes back into the hole. A pocket of bagged soil can keep roots circling in it instead of reaching into the surrounding ground. Kilgore's sandy topsoil backfills easily, and mulch on top does more good than amendments underneath.

faq.q: Do you check on the tree after planting?
faq.a: You get a written watering schedule with every planting. On bigger installs we come back around the 30-day mark to check how the tree is establishing. Between visits, a trickle from the hose at the root ball is the single best thing you can do for it.

tree-shrub-care.local_h: Pruning shrubs and small trees in the shade of big ones
local: Under Kilgore's mature pecans and post oaks, the understory takes a beating. Shrubs and small trees compete for light, lean toward every gap in the canopy and end up lopsided. We prune for shape and health, cut out dead wood and open up the plants that have grown into a wall or a roofline. On a typical Kilgore lot that means a walk around the yard, a plant-by-plant list of what needs work and what should be left alone, and a written quote.

Crepe myrtles are the plant that most often gets cut wrong. We thin them in February while they are dormant and before the buds break, and we do not top them. Topping leaves knuckles and a crop of weak shoots that flop under the weight of the blooms. A tree already topped can be recovered, but it takes two or three winters, so we plan the work out and come back each dormant season to finish it.

Oaks get different timing. Oak wilt is a real concern in East Texas, and the beetles that carry it are drawn to fresh pruning cuts in spring and early summer, so the post oaks in Kilgore are left alone then. Dead lower limbs get cleared off shade trees, cuts go at the branch collar, and when a limb comes down in a storm we cut it clean and haul it away. A big pine or pecan leaning over a roof is not a job we take on.

Small trees and shrubs that have outgrown their spot can come out, and the trimmings get raked and hauled before we leave. We also do seasonal fertilizer feeding for trees and shrubs and a mulch refresh around tree bases, which helps in Kilgore's fast-draining sand. A tree that sits at a corner of the house gets the same careful look as the one in the back. Pricing follows the count, the size and condition of each plant and how much debris there is.

faq.q: How much does tree and shrub care cost in Kilgore?
faq.a: We do not publish a price, because a light shaping on a few shrubs is a very different job from recovering a row of topped crepe myrtles. The walkthrough is free and you get a written, itemized quote, usually within a day. The count of plants, their size and condition, any removals and the debris to haul off set the number.

faq.q: Will you top my crepe myrtles?
faq.a: No. Topping leaves knuckles and weak shoots that flop under the blooms. We thin crepe myrtles in late winter instead, cutting back to a branch or the trunk, so the tree keeps a natural shape and blooms well. If yours was already topped, we can plan its recovery over two or three winters.

faq.q: When can the post oaks in my Kilgore yard be pruned?
faq.a: Not in spring or early summer. Oak wilt beetles are drawn to fresh cuts in that window, so we prune oaks in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer. Storm-broken limbs are the exception. Those get a clean cut and are hauled away right away.

faq.q: Can you take down a large pine or pecan near my house?
faq.a: No. We remove small trees and shrubs that have outgrown their spot, but a large tree close to a house is not work we take on. At the walkthrough we will tell you which trees fall inside what we do and which are better left to a different kind of crew.

faq.q: Do you feed trees and shrubs as well as prune them?
faq.a: Yes. Seasonal fertilizer feeding for trees and shrubs is part of the service, along with a mulch refresh around tree bases. Kilgore's sandy, acidic soil lets nutrients wash through quickly, so feeding is worth discussing at the walkthrough along with the pruning.
